title: Mistä: answering with -lta and -ltä
summary: Mistä also asks where from with the at/on family. Mistä sinä tulet? — Tulen asemalta.
objectives: Use mistä to ask for a source in the at/on place family.
Answer with the appropriate -lta or -ltä source form.

sections.title: Meaning and pattern
paragraphs: Singular refers to one person or one thing in these patterns.
Plural means more than one in this grammatical pattern.
A stem is the part of a word to which an ending is attached.
The elative is the from-inside form, answering where from.
Mistä also asks where from with the at/on family. Change the taught location's -lla/-llä to -lta/-ltä: asemalla (“at the station”) becomes asemalta (“from the station”).
keyPoints: Keep mistä for the source even when the location uses the -lla family.

sections.title: Answering the question
paragraphs: Answer the source, not the destination: Tulen torilta (“I am coming from the market square”). A source phrase such as Torilta is enough as a short reply. The complete verb forms are supplied; this lesson chooses the source relationship.
A natural short reply to “Mistä sinä tulet?” is “Asemalta.” (“From the station.”). Use the full reply when it makes the person, action or correction clearer.
Keep the source relationship while rejecting the incorrect source. The second sentence supplies the actual source, so the reply answers mistä.
The exercises show supporting Finnish words and their meanings when recalling them is not the task. Read the complete English meaning before choosing the question or answer form.
keyPoints: Use -lta/-ltä for these sources rather than -lla/-llä or -lle.

sections.title: Build the answer forms
paragraphs: asemalta means from the station here. Asema + -lta gives asemalta.
torilta means from the market square here. Tori + -lta gives torilta.
pihalta means from the yard here. Piha + -lta gives pihalta.
pöydältä means from the table here. Pöytä changes t to d before -ltä: pöydältä.
tuolilta means from the chair here. Tuoli + -lta gives tuolilta.
keyPoints: Use -lta/-ltä for these sources rather than -lla/-llä or -lle.

steps: Mistä: where from; question asking where from. Mistä is the elative question form and asks for the source.
sinä: you; subject (who or what this sentence is about). Sinä addresses one person informally.
tulet: you come; verb (the action or state). Use the stem tule- and singular second-person -t: tulet.

examples.english: I am coming from the station.
steps: Tulen: I come; verb (the action or state). Tulla removes -la and adds e to form tule-, then adds -n: tulen.
asemalta: from the station; source. Asema + -lta gives asemalta.
Mistä: where from; question asking where from. Mistä is the elative question form and asks for the source.
hän: he or she; subject (who or what this sentence is about). Hän refers to one other person without specifying gender.
tulee: comes; verb (the action or state). Use tule- and lengthen the final e: tulee.

examples.english: Where are they taking the book from?
steps: Mistä: where from; question asking where from. Mistä is the elative question form and asks for the source.
he: they; subject (who or what this sentence is about). He refers to other people; this is Finnish plural he.
ottavat: take; verb (the action or state). Strong otta- + plural third-person -vat gives ottavat.
kirjan: the book; object (the thing the action concerns). Kirja + -n gives kirjan, the supplied total object of this bounded taking or placing action.

examples.english: I am not coming from the station. I am coming from the market square.
steps: En: I do not; negative verb (marks not and identifies the person). En is the first-person singular negative verb. The main verb takes its negative form.
tule: come; main verb after the negative verb. Remove -n from tulen to obtain the negative main-verb form tule; the negative verb carries the person.

Tulen: I come; verb (the action or state). Tulla removes -la and adds e to form tule-, then adds -n: tulen.
torilta: from the market square; source. Tori + -lta gives torilta.
